title: More the Merrier
synopsis: Your in-laws, three exes, a missionary cousin, and an estranged sibling all confirm for Thanksgiving. You have one oven and one nerve left. Cook.

nodes.text: Twenty names on the legal pad. You count them twice, because the second count usually helps. The oven manual, which you have now read for pleasure, says the capacity is comfortable for fifteen. Under the last name you have drawn a small question mark, and the question mark is doing a lot of work.

choices.consequence: You cross off your uncle's second wife, then put her back, then cross off nobody. The list is still twenty and the pencil is now a casualty.
You text the neighbors asking to rent oven space like a woman arranging a crime. Deb says yes and asks only for a plate of dark meat.

nodes.text: Anita replies to the group thread with one word: 'Coming.' Seven years of Thanksgivings without her, and the woman commits in six letters. You put the phone face down on the counter. You pick it back up. You read the word again to see whether it has changed. It has not.

choices.consequence: You call. It rings four times, she picks up, and the first thing either of you says out loud is about parking.
You add a chair and don't call. Planning is a way of loving people from a distance, and you are excellent at it.

nodes.text: Your spouse's ex, Dana, is coming, because the custody math dropped the kids here on the fourth Thursday and the kids are non-negotiable. Dana brings a pumpkin roll every year. The pumpkin roll is genuinely excellent. This has been the central unfairness of your marriage for six years running.

choices.consequence: You draw a chart. Dana lands at the far corner near the kids, which reads as thoughtful and is, mostly, thoughtful.
You decide seating charts are for cowards. You will revisit this position at 4:15 p.m. with a serving spoon in your fist.

nodes.text: Cousin Joel has landed from Phnom Penh with a duffel bag and a laminated photo of a well he helped dig. He would like to say a short prayer before the meal. Joel's last short prayer ran twenty-two minutes and included a slideshow. He did not bring the projector. He mentions this twice.

choices.consequence: You ask him for four minutes. Joel agrees to four minutes the way a jazz musician agrees to a set list.
You let it go. Somewhere in your chest a small realistic voice begins timing the gravy against the Book of Ruth.

nodes.text: Mom wants the green bean casserole. Not a green bean casserole — the one with the canned soup and the fried onions from the specific brand, in the specific dish, on her plate, in a portion she describes using her hands. She has emailed you about it. The email had an attachment.

choices.consequence: You make it exactly as specified, brand included. Surrender is a legitimate culinary technique and this one takes nine minutes.
You try haricots verts with shallots. It's the better dish. Nobody has ever wanted the better dish in the history of this holiday.

nodes.text: Three in the afternoon on the Tuesday before, and the store has become a weather event. A man stands in front of the butter with the stillness of someone rethinking his life. Two carts have interlocked near the pies and no one is addressing it. Somewhere a child is being taught about scarcity.

choices.consequence: Your list is organized by aisle and color-coded and you still forget the celery. You forget the celery every single year.
You come home with four cheeses, no stock, and a decorative gourd. The gourd was a decision you made on purpose.

nodes.text: Anita leaves a voicemail at 6:40 in the morning, which is when she has always called. 'Bringing Steve,' she says. 'He eats anything.' Steve is the man she was supposed to marry seven years ago, in the church, with the deposit already paid. You play the message for your spouse. Your spouse sits down.

choices.consequence: You text back 'Great — we'll set two.' It takes you twenty minutes to write and reads, correctly, as effortless.
You ask, gently, whether she's sure. She sends a thumbs up, which is either serenity or the end of the conversation.

nodes.text: Your spouse is handling it. Your spouse has been handling it so thoroughly that they are now alphabetizing the spice drawer at nine at night while explaining, in a completely level voice, that everything is under control. The oregano is up front. You have spent four days managing an event and zero minutes managing a person.

choices.consequence: You shut the drawer and ask an actual question. They cry for about ninety seconds, then alphabetize anyway, but happier.
You say 'almost there' and hand them a whisk. It works tonight. It also gets filed somewhere and reopened in February.

nodes.text: The final arithmetic, done on an envelope: two ovens counting Deb's next door, plus a toaster oven with ambitions. One spatchcocked turkey. Two hours forty, door to plate, assuming the bird cooperates and nobody opens anything to look. Somebody will open something to look. Statistically, that somebody is your mother.

choices.consequence: You break the bird's spine with kitchen shears and a sound the dog does not enjoy. It cooks in half the time.
You buy a backup turkey. Redundant, expensive, and the single calmest decision anyone in this house makes all week.

nodes.text: Pies on Tuesday night, because Wednesday belongs to other people. Apple, pumpkin, and one pecan you are making purely out of spite toward a man who isn't even coming. The crust turns out beautifully: cold butter, a marble board, and forty uninterrupted minutes of nobody speaking to you. Radio low. This is the good part.

choices.consequence: You bake a fourth at midnight for no defensible reason. It will be the one that vanishes first tomorrow.
Three pies, twenty people. You do the slice math, look at the slice math, and decide the slice math is Thursday's problem.

nodes.text: Anita climbs out of a rented Corolla holding a houseplant she has clearly kept alive on purpose. Steve unloads the trunk without being asked. She hugs you in the driveway before either of you has said anything, and she is smaller than you remember, and you understand that you have been telling yourself a story for seven years.

choices.consequence: You hug her back with both arms and hold it one beat past comfortable. Steve looks politely at the hedge.
You hug her the way you'd hug a colleague at a conference. She notices. She lets you have it, which is worse.

nodes.text: Your in-laws arrive with the wrong wine again. It's a Barolo. It is objectively lovely, costs more than your shoes, goes with nothing whatsoever on the menu, and its price will be mentioned within four minutes of the cork leaving the bottle. Your father-in-law is already holding the corkscrew.

choices.consequence: You open it Wednesday with cheese and crackers, where it makes no sense at all and everyone adores it. Problem dissolved.
You shelve it with a compliment. Your mother-in-law's face performs a very small, very fast calculation and then resets.

nodes.text: Five children now occupy the house, ages three through twelve, distributed across the floor like a dropped puzzle. The twelve-year-old has become a vegetarian. She became one this morning. She is extremely calm about it and has printed no materials, which somehow makes it harder to argue with. Her mother mouths 'sorry' across the kitchen.

choices.consequence: You pull the bacon out of the Brussels sprouts. Four adults notice within the hour and every one of them says something.
You build a mushroom galette at ten at night. She eats two slices and calls it fine, which from a twelve-year-old is a rave.

nodes.text: Five-thirty. The turkey goes in with a sound like a door closing on a long project. Coffee. The house sleeps in every direction, the kitchen window goes black to grey to that particular gold, and for about ten minutes you are one person alone in a warm room with something roasting. Nobody needs anything from you.

choices.text: Sit at the window for ten minutes
choices.consequence: You sit. You drink the coffee hot, all the way to the bottom, for the first time since September. Then a child materializes.
You start the rolls instead and get a full half-hour ahead of schedule, all of which you will surrender again by nine.

nodes.text: It takes forty seconds. Your mother remarks that the onions were 'a choice.' Your spouse answers while holding a knife, which changes the register of the room considerably. And then Anita — who has been back in this family for one day — asks your mother to show her how it's supposed to be done, and the whole thing is over.

choices.consequence: You thank her at the table, out loud, in front of everyone. Anita turns a color you last saw on her at fourteen.
You catch her eye across the kitchen and lift your chin half an inch. She lifts hers back. That's the deal.

nodes.text: Twenty people, one long table plus a card table pretending to be part of it, and every face has turned toward you holding a glass. You had something prepared on your phone. The phone is in the other room, in a coat pocket, under a sleeping dog. You are going to have to mean this live.

choices.consequence: You say the thing about the empty chair not being empty anymore. Two people set their forks down. Nobody chews for a second.
Nine words and a joke about the oven. It lands, it stops, and everyone gets to eat while the food is hot.

nodes.text: Joel prays for six minutes, which for Joel is a haiku. He covers the food, the farmers, and the truck drivers. Then he says Anita's name out loud, and Steve's, like they've always been on the list. Anita's eyes are shut, but not in the normal way. Steve reaches over without looking and takes her hand.

choices.consequence: You take the other one. She grips back hard enough to hurt, and neither of you mentions it — not then, not ever.

choices.text: Pretend not to notice the tear
choices.consequence: You study the tablecloth with tremendous interest. Sometimes the kindest thing available to a person is a tablecloth.

nodes.text: Everything reaches the table hot at the same moment, which has never once happened before and will not happen again. Turkey juicy. Rolls on time. The casserole sits on your mother's plate: correct brand, correct dish, correct portion. She eats all of it and says absolutely nothing about it, and that is the thank-you.

choices.consequence: You sit. It takes your body four minutes to believe you, and then the whole week arrives at once and flattens you.
You stay standing and work the table with the Barolo. Your father-in-law announces the price. Right on schedule, to the minute.

nodes.text: Dana makes a small joke about the gravy and the entire table laughs, your spouse included, you included. Across from her the kids stop tracking which parent they're supposed to be sitting near. For roughly one minute they belong to a single house instead of two, and not one of them notices it happening.

choices.consequence: You catch your spouse's eye and tip your head toward the kids. They see it. A hand lands on your knee under the table.
You say nothing and pass the potatoes. Certain things get smaller the instant somebody points a finger at them.

nodes.text: Anita washes, you dry, and it takes an hour because neither of you is trying to finish. You talk about a dog you had in 1998 and a teacher you both hated and, somewhere around the roasting pan, about the wedding. Not a big conversation. A long one. Seven years close like a drawer.

choices.consequence: You ask about Christmas before you can talk yourself out of it. She says 'yeah, okay' to the sink, fast, like she'd been waiting.

choices.text: Take it one holiday at a time
choices.consequence: Neither of you says a word about December. Both of you are already quietly counting the weeks until December.

nodes.text: Half past midnight. The house has gone soft — somebody's cousin asleep under a throw, the dishwasher grinding through its second run. One wedge of apple pie left in the tin. You and your spouse stand at the island in the dark with two forks and the annual debate over whether this counts as breakfast.

choices.consequence: You eat it standing up straight out of the tin, and it is better than any slice served on a plate all day.
You cover it in foil and go to bed. At six the foil is on the counter and the tin is empty and no one confesses.
Neither of you reaches for a fork. There is a thing you have both been circling since the driveway, and it is not dessert.

nodes.text: Anita comes for Christmas. Then Easter, then a random Tuesday in June with no occasion attached to it at all. The family gets bigger and, against every available prediction, easier. Steve turns out to be the man who fixes your gutters. And two Novembers later your mother asks Anita for her casserole recipe — Anita's, not the one on the soup can — and asks in front of everybody, which is the entire apology.

Next November you go small on purpose: your house, Anita, Steve, and nobody who has ever described a wine as an investment. Eight people. One oven, used once. You sit down at two in the afternoon and are still at that table at six because there is nowhere else to be. Joel calls from Cambodia and prays over speakerphone for nineteen minutes, and you let him, because he is not in your kitchen.

Years later you make a book of it. Spiral-bound, forty copies, printed at a strip-mall shop by a man named Curtis who did not charge you nearly enough. Mom's casserole is page two, dictated word for word, brand name included. Joel gets a full chapter titled 'Grace (Abridged).' Anita writes the introduction, and it runs four paragraphs, and it wrecks every one of you out loud at the table, every year.
